title: About the CIA Challenge Exam
description: What the CIA Challenge Exam looks like, who sits it, where its topics come from in the three CIA parts, how to read its questions from the right seat, how to pace and prepare, how to book it, and what follows. Written in plain language by KaiSip from The IIA's published information.
disclaimer: Certified Internal Auditor® and CIA® are registered trademarks, and Global Internal Audit Standards™ is a trademark, of The IIA (The Institute of Internal Auditors, Inc.). CISA® is a registered trademark of ISACA. KaiSip is an independent study aid. It is not affiliated with, sponsored, endorsed or licensed by The IIA, and it is not affiliated with or endorsed by ISACA. All notes and questions are written by KaiSip; none are actual exam questions. The IIA alone sets the exam rules and decides eligibility and certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: Fees, dates, windows, languages and rules on this page were checked on the date shown. They can change, so check theiia.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: The CIA Challenge Exam is one exam of 150 multiple-choice questions in 180 minutes, taken on a computer at a Pearson VUE test center in set testing windows. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
items: 150 multiple-choice questions in 180 minutes: 1.2 minutes, or 72 seconds, a question on average. That is three hours in one sitting.
It is a separate route into the CIA program for people on one of The IIA's Challenge pathways, in place of the three exam parts. Every pathway sits the same exam on the same syllabus.
Its 40 topics come from all three CIA parts: a few from Part 1 and every topic of Parts 2 and 3. The section on where the topics come from shows the match.
Outside mainland China, the exam runs only in February, June, September and November, and you book a seat inside one of those testing windows. Mainland China has single test days instead.
The IIA's published sample questions each have four options, A to D. KaiSip's practice questions use the same shape, with one best answer.
Scores are reported on a scale from 250 to 750, and 600 or higher passes. 600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions.
Wrong answers are not penalized, so answer every question, including the ones you are unsure of.
No breaks are scheduled. You may step away, but the clock keeps running.
You sit the exam in person at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
The exam is non-disclosed: The IIA does not publish current questions and answers. Every KaiSip question is written by KaiSip, and none is a real exam question.
The exam rests on the Global Internal Audit Standards, published on 9 January 2024 and effective from 9 January 2025.

sections.title: Who sits the Challenge Exam
sections.summary: The Challenge Exam is for people The IIA has approved on one of its Challenge pathways. Each pathway has its own entry rules, and all of them sit the same exam.
items: Accounting pathway: holders of an approved certified public accountant (CPA) or chartered accountant (CA) credential.
Information systems pathway: holders of an active CISA®. The next section, Coming from CISA, sets out this route's entry rules and what changes for you.

Professional pathway: a pilot for people with 10 or more years of experience. Its applications are closed, only those who applied by 30 September 2026 may register, and The IIA is reviewing whether it continues.
The pilot's testing windows are November 2026 and February 2027. If you are in the pilot, check your own window with The IIA.
Every pathway uses the same exam content and the same syllabus, so this course is the same whichever pathway brought you here.
The CIA program, Challenge route included, must be completed within 3 years of approval.

sections.title: Coming from CISA
sections.summary: The Challenge Exam is one exam for every pathway, active CISA® holders included. Much of your engagement skill carries over; running the function, the board's part, quality and results are new. KaiSip's bridge notes map each difference.
items: CISA holders apply with an active CISA, a government photo ID and a public-registry record showing the credential in good standing. No proof of experience is asked, and applications are open all year.

Every pathway sits the same exam on the same syllabus: 150 questions in 180 minutes, offered in the February, June, September and November testing windows (mainland China has single test days instead).
A registration stays valid for 180 days, or less if your program ends sooner, and there are no extensions. You may sit the exam up to eight times in all within the three-year program.
Sections C and D, 45% together, reuse the most CISA skill: planning, evidence, testing, workpapers and findings. Learn The IIA's words for them, and who approves each step.

Sections A, B and E, 55% together, are mostly new: the mandate and charter, roles beyond internal auditing, quality, the strategy, budget and plan, risk acceptance and follow-up, mostly from the chief audit executive's seat.

Habits that cost marks: answering as the IT specialist, treating the board and senior management as one audience, doing the chief audit executive's part yourself, and stopping at 'report it to the audit committee'.

Also watch for: taking a framework as the criteria before asking what the board and senior management have set, using another body's evidence, risk and opinion words, turning a should into a must, and running advisory work exactly like assurance.
Read every option in The IIA's 2024 terms: internal auditor, board, activity under review, work program, relevant, reliable and sufficient information, engagement conclusion and action plan.
KaiSip's Coming from CISA notes take each section in turn and keep the CISA comparison apart, in a labeled table and one exam trap per lesson, so every lesson also reads on its own.
CISA® is a registered trademark of ISACA, named here only to say who this section is for. KaiSip is independent: not affiliated with or endorsed by ISACA or The IIA.

sections.title: The five sections and their weights
sections.summary: The IIA's Challenge syllabus splits the exam into five sections. A section's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a fair guide to where your study time goes.

domains.name: Internal Audit Operations and Audit Plan

items: Section D, Engagement Performance, is the largest at 25%: sources and quality of evidence, analytics, findings and their causes, workpapers, conclusions, and supervising and communicating while the work is under way.

Section A, Internal Audit Professionalism and Quality, is 20%: the mandate, independence, the Three Lines Model, individual objectivity, confidentiality, the quality program, nonconformance and performance measures.
Section C, Engagement Planning, is 20%: objectives and scope, criteria, key risks and controls with fraud basics, the approach, the engagement risk assessment, the work program and resources.
Section E, Engagement Results and Monitoring, is 20%: the final communication, recommendations and action plans, residual risk, risk that management accepts, and following up and escalating actions.

Section B is the smallest at 15%. It covers running the function and its plan: methodologies, the budget, people and technology, the strategy, reporting to the board, the risk-based plan and other assurance providers.
The syllabus lists 40 numbered topics: 8 in Section A, 7 in B, 7 in C, 10 in D and 8 in E. KaiSip's codes start with 4 for this fourth exam, so 4E6 is Section E, topic 6.

sections.title: Where the 40 topics come from
sections.summary: Every Challenge topic has the same wording as a topic in one of the three CIA parts. KaiSip matched them line by line, so you know which notes teach each topic and which seat to answer from.
items: Part 1, Internal Audit Fundamentals: 5 of its 27 topics, all in Section A. They are the mandate, threats to independence, the Three Lines Model, individual objectivity, and confidentiality.
Part 2, Internal Audit Engagement: all 17 topics. Its planning topics form Section C; evidence, analysis, findings, workpapers, conclusions, supervision and communication form Section D.
Part 3, Internal Audit Function: all 18 topics. Quality and performance measures join Section A, operations and the plan form Section B, and results and monitoring form Section E.
One line exists only in the Challenge syllabus: Section C's topic on key risks and controls adds fraud basics, the fraud triangle and common schemes. The three-part exam teaches these in Part 1.
Most of Part 1 is not a Challenge topic: governance, risk management and control concepts, most of ethics, and fraud beyond the basics. KaiSip's reading: questions can still assume the basic ideas.
If each section's weight is spread evenly over its topics, a KaiSip working assumption and not an IIA figure, Part 1 topics are about 12.5% of the exam, Part 2 about 45% and Part 3 about 42.5%.
The match is KaiSip's comparison of the syllabus files labeled V2.10.2025 FINAL (Challenge) and V2.09.2024 FINAL (the parts). It is not a statement from The IIA.

sections.title: What the syllabus verbs tell you
sections.summary: The syllabus gives no depth label for a topic. Each topic line starts with a verb, and that verb signals how deep its questions can go. The three groups below are KaiSip's reading.
items: Know and explain (Describe, Recognize, Identify, Explain): 20 of the 40 topics, most of them in Sections A, B and E. Expect the right rule, role or step, often inside a short scenario.
Use it (Interpret, Apply, Demonstrate, Maintain): 6 topics, four of them in Section D, such as analytics, supervision and communication. Expect a situation and the question of how to handle it well.
Weigh and decide (Determine, Evaluate, Plan and similar verbs): 14 topics, among them all seven in Section C and five in Section D. Expect several reasonable moves and one that fits best.
So the engagement sections, C and D, carry most of the judgment, while A, B and E mostly test who does what in the function. Both still arrive as scenarios.
A topic's detail lines can go deeper than its verb. Practice until you can say why the closest wrong choice loses, not only which answer is right.

sections.title: Syllabus, languages and Topical Requirements
sections.summary: One current syllabus serves every pathway. KaiSip teaches it and the 2024 Standards, not the older exam and its vocabulary.
items: The current Challenge syllabus took effect on 1 June 2026; its file is labeled V2.10.2025 FINAL. Older books and many free notes still teach earlier vocabulary; KaiSip does not.
The Challenge Exam is offered in English, French and Spanish, and in Simplified Chinese in mainland China only, with exams from December 2026.
In mainland China, single test days take the place of the windows. The 2026 days are 8 March, 7 June, 6 September and 6 December.

Five Challenge topics ask you to recognize when a Topical Requirement applies: in the quality program (4A6), the audit universe (4B5), and engagement objectives, planning and risk assessment (4C1, 4C3, 4C5).
Assurance work on a Topical Requirement's topic must conform, advisory work is recommended to, and any exclusion is recorded with its reason.
Topical Requirements enter the exam on dates. Scored questions on a new one do not appear until at least 6 months after it takes effect.

Cybersecurity is testable now. When checked, The IIA's CIA exam reference list also named Third-Party from March 2027, Organizational Behavior from June 2027 and Organizational Resilience from October 2027.
KaiSip found no separate testing dates for the Challenge Exam. Before you rely on these months, confirm with The IIA which dates apply to your window.
A fifth, Anti-Corruption, was issued on 23 November 2026 and takes effect on 23 November 2027. Under the six-month policy no scored question on it can appear before 23 May 2028.

sections.title: Read each question from the right seat
sections.summary: A Challenge question gives you a seat through the topic it tests. Find the seat first, then the actor and the strength of the rule. These are KaiSip's habits, built on the Standards.
steps: Read the last line first. Note what is asked for: an action, a person, a document, a test or a reason.
Name the seat from the topic: the mandate, independence or objectivity, one engagement, or the function as a whole. Each puts you in a different chair.
Find the actor: an internal auditor, the engagement supervisor, the chief audit executive, the board, senior management, the management of the activity, or another provider.

Find the priority word, such as “first”, “best” or “most”, written in lowercase, and the strength: does the question ask what is required (a must), what is good practice (a should), or what comes first?
Rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, often two. Settle the last two by asking who approves, who must be told and in what order, and who owns the action.
Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice. Then answer and move on.
items: Part 1 topics, in Section A: an internal auditor who knows the rules and who does what. The board grants the mandate, the function stays independent, each auditor stays objective, and information serves the work only.

Part 2 topics, in Sections C and D: the internal auditor running one engagement under a supervisor. Understand the activity and its risks, set objectives, scope and criteria, get the work program approved, then test and conclude.

Part 3 topics, in Sections A, B and E: the chief audit executive running the function. You propose, manage, report and escalate; the board approves and oversees; senior management gives input; management owns risks and actions.
A common trap is an option from the wrong seat: one engagement's fieldwork step when the question is about the function, or a board decision when only one engagement is at stake.

Not the IT specialist, not the external auditor, not the risk owner, not the manager. Configuring a system, an opinion on the financial statements, choosing the risk response and fixing the problem belong to others.

“Primary” asks for the main purpose and “most likely” for probability, not severity. CIA questions usually ask for the right answer; if you meet “least”, flip the test. The full list of priority words is on the final review week's cheat sheet.

sections.title: Who approves, who is told, and when
sections.summary: Across all three seats, many questions turn on who approves, who must be told, and in what order. These are KaiSip's patterns, built on the Standards. The first three are the traps KaiSip's question reviews kept finding.
items: Board approval only where a Standard asks for it, such as the charter, the plan and its significant changes, the budget, the resource plan, the performance objectives and the external assessment plan. The strategy is reviewed, not approved.

"Tell the board promptly" is not always the answer. Accepted risk goes to the responsible management and senior management before the board, failed coordination goes to senior management first, and a scope limitation is discussed with management first.

A should can come first. Asked what is required, a should loses to a must. Asked what to do first, the should step can win: raising accepted risk with the responsible management comes before senior management.

Mandate and charter: the chief audit executive supplies the information and drafts the charter, senior management gives input, and the board grants the mandate and approves the charter (Standards 6.1, 6.2).

Independence and objectivity: the chief audit executive confirms the function's independence to the board at least yearly. Objectivity is each auditor's own; an impairment is disclosed first, then safeguarded (Standards 2.3, 7.1).

One engagement: the chief audit executive or a delegated supervisor approves the objectives, scope and work program, and changes to them, before the work goes on. Criteria start from what the board and senior management set (Standards 13.3, 13.4, 13.6).

Evidence and findings: information that is relevant, reliable and sufficient; the condition compared with the criteria; the root cause found with management where possible; significance weighed by likelihood and impact (Standards 14.1 to 14.3).
Plan gaps and money: resource limits and high-risk areas left without assurance go in time to the board and senior management (Standards 9.4, 10.1). Here telling is the must, not approval.

Quality: internal assessment results go to the board and senior management at least yearly. The board receives an external assessment's complete results directly from the assessor (Standards 8.3, 8.4).

Results: internal auditors draft; the chief audit executive approves the final communication before issue and decides who receives it. A significant error is corrected for everyone who received it (Standards 11.3, 11.4, 15.1).

Accepted risk above appetite or tolerance: the responsible management first (a should), senior management (a must), then the board if unresolved (a must). The chief audit executive never resolves the risk (Standard 11.5).

Follow-up: management implements and internal auditors confirm. A missed date goes, with management's explanation, to the chief audit executive, who judges whether risk beyond tolerance has been accepted (Standard 15.2).

sections.title: Common traps by section
sections.summary: Each section has a few traps that catch prepared candidates. Most answer from the wrong seat, ask for an approval no Standard requires, or call a should a must. These are KaiSip's patterns, organized by The IIA's sections.
items: Professionalism: treating independence and objectivity as one. Independence is the function's place in the organization; objectivity is each auditor's mind, and a sound reporting line never proves that one person is unbiased.

Professionalism: giving assurance on an area you ran within the past 12 months, trusting your own care. Objectivity is presumed impaired, and the duty to refrain has no time limit; disclose it, and expect to be reassigned.

Quality: claiming conformance without support, or keeping a nonconformance quiet. A conformance statement needs supervision and the quality program behind it; a nonconformance is disclosed with its impact.

Operations: seeking the board's approval of the strategy as if a Standard required it, or trimming the plan quietly when money runs short. The strategy is reviewed; a shortfall's impact goes promptly to the board and senior management.

Plan: treating a senior manager's request as an order, or relying on another provider because of its reputation. A request is an input to the risk assessment; reliance follows evaluation and a documented basis.

Planning: letting the management of the activity set an assurance engagement's scope, or dropping a Topical Requirement because management prefers it. Internal auditors set the scope, the chief audit executive approves it, and any exclusion is recorded with its reason.

Planning: considering fraud only after a tip, or starting fieldwork while the work program waits for approval. Fraud risk belongs in every engagement risk assessment, and approval comes before testing.

Performance: treating an interview or a self-assessment as proof that a control operates, or an analytics flag as a finding. Statements describe; inspection and data show; a flag is a lead until follow-up.

Performance: naming the symptom as the root cause, or a supervisor rewriting a conclusion without asking for more evidence. Ask why until you reach a cause, and let the evidence settle the conclusion.

Results: deleting a finding management fixed before issue, or softening a conclusion because management disagrees. The fix is acknowledged and the finding stays; record both positions and change a result only for a valid reason.

Monitoring: telling the board first when management accepts too much risk, or closing an action because its date has passed. The route runs through management first, and nothing closes until internal audit confirms it.

sections.title: Pacing your 180 minutes
sections.summary: 180 minutes for 150 questions is 1.2 minutes each. Use that number to set two checkpoints, not to time every question.
items: Checkpoints: reach question 75 by minute 90; reach question 125 by minute 150. Look at the clock at those two points and otherwise leave it alone.
Three hours is long. Stamina matters as much as speed, so sit your full mock in one unbroken session at the real length.
Ahead at a checkpoint? The minutes you have saved are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few questions instead of rushing all of them.
If a question stalls you, choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess beats a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one. Plan as if you will sit straight through.
A long scenario takes more than the average and a plain rule question takes less, so judge your pace at the checkpoints, never on one question.

sections.title: Your score and KaiSip's numbers
sections.summary: The IIA reports a scaled score. KaiSip never shows one: it shows the percent you got right, by section, and its own readiness band. The two are different things.
items: The IIA converts your raw score to a reporting scale that runs from 250 to 750. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions. KaiSip knows of no published way to turn a percent correct into a scaled score, and it does not try.
If you pass, your score report shows no number at all. If you do not, it shows your score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
A KaiSip mock result shows your percent correct for each section and your pace against the checkpoints. It is labeled as KaiSip's, and it is not The IIA's score.
KaiSip's readiness band is its own summary of your practice. It is a study signal, not a prediction of your result.
A good use of a practice percent: compare your five sections with each other and with last week, and give time to the section furthest behind its weight.

sections.title: Your last week before the exam
sections.summary: A calm seven-day plan with nothing new in it: one full timed mock early, then your slips, the section sheets and the close pairs, and rest at the end.
steps: Seven days out: sit one full timed mock of 150 questions in 180 minutes, using the two checkpoints. This is your last full mock before the exam.
Six days out: review each miss and name the thinking slip behind it. Then recall Section D, the largest section, and the three tests for evidence. Stop at about 90 minutes.
Five days out: the three close pairs (approve or tell, must or should, function or engagement), then Section A and a short untimed set in your weakest section.
Four days out: one short timed mock. Then recall Section C in engagement order, the work program's approval, and why fraud risk is always assessed.
Three days out: Sections E and B, the route for a missed action date, and a redo of your mistake journal. No timed tests from today on.
Two days out: light review. Say the priority words and the answering routine from memory, then check. Confirm your appointment, ID and route.
One day out: rest. Glance at your own short list of rules, get ready for the morning, and sleep at your usual time.
items: Nothing new this week. The plan sharpens what you already know; a topic you have never studied is better left alone now.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with the next one. Never double up.
Recall beats rereading: answer from memory first, then check.
Coming from CISA? Some days also name a lesson from the Coming from CISA notes. Candidates on other pathways can skip those lines.
Practice results in any study app, including KaiSip, are not The IIA's scaled scores and cannot predict your result.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You apply on your Challenge pathway, register for the exam, then book a seat at a Pearson VUE test center in a testing window. The IIA's prices change on 4 January 2027.
steps: Check that you qualify for a Challenge pathway: accounting, information systems or, if you applied by 30 September 2026, the professional pilot.
Apply and pay the application fee. Once you are approved, you have 3 years to complete the program.
Register for the exam and pay its fee. A registration lasts 180 days, or less if your program ends sooner.
Book a Pearson VUE test center appointment inside those 180 days: in a February, June, September or November window, or on a mainland China test day.
items: Until 3 January 2027: application fee US$150 for IIA members and US$380 for non-members; Challenge exam fee US$845 for members and US$1,245 for non-members.
From 4 January 2027: application fee US$185 for members and US$245 for non-members; Challenge exam fee US$995 for members and US$1,335 for non-members.
These are The IIA's listed prices for the United States, Canada and some other countries. Where a national institute of The IIA runs the exams, prices may differ.
Fees are not refunded and cannot be transferred.
The Challenge route has no extensions, of the program or of a registration. Time your registration so that its 180 days hold the window you want.
You can change an appointment up to 48 hours before it. Pearson VUE charges US$75 each time.

sections.title: Test center only
sections.summary: The exam is taken in person, on a computer, at a Pearson VUE test center, in the testing windows or, in mainland China, on single test days. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
items: There is no at-home or online option. Advice that mentions remote testing for this exam is out of date.

Outside mainland China, the exam runs only in February, June, September and November. Pick a window inside your 180-day registration, then a test center and a time of day, and book early enough to get them.
In mainland China, single test days take the place of the windows. The section on syllabus and languages lists the 2026 days.
You can move the appointment up to 48 hours before it, for a Pearson VUE fee of US$75 each time.
The check-in, ID and test-room rules are for The IIA and Pearson VUE to set. Read them in the current candidate handbook and in your appointment confirmation; KaiSip does not restate them.
Plan the trip ahead: know the route, the travel time and a backup, so nothing about the morning is left to chance.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Arrive with time in hand, pace by your two checkpoints, and answer every question. Three hours is long, so settle in for one sitting.
items: Bring what The IIA's candidate handbook and your appointment confirmation tell you to bring. Check the ID rules a few days ahead, while there is still time to fix a problem.
150 questions in 180 minutes. Checkpoints: question 75 by minute 90; question 125 by minute 150.
No breaks are scheduled. If you take one, the clock keeps running.
Answer every question. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess always beats a blank.
For each question: read the last line, name the seat from the topic, find the actor and the priority word, rule out two options, then settle the final two with a principle.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and return to it if time allows.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: You do not see a score when you finish. Since the September 2026 window, the official Challenge result arrives within 3 weeks of your exam date.
items: No immediate unofficial score is shown. Official results arrive within 3 weeks of the exam date.
A pass report shows no numeric score. A report for an exam that was not passed shows the score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
If you did not pass, you can sit the exam again in a later testing window, up to eight attempts in all within your 3-year program.
The program's 3-year clock keeps running, and the Challenge route has no extensions, so plan any retake with the window dates in view.
Treat a report that lists areas to improve as a study map: start with the areas it names, then compare them with your KaiSip section percents.

sections.title: Becoming certified
sections.summary: On the Challenge route, the exam is the step this course prepares you for. The IIA decides every application and grants the certification.
items: Pass the Challenge Exam within 3 years of your program approval.
On the information systems pathway, no proof of experience is asked when you apply; you show an active CISA® in good standing instead.
KaiSip has not checked the steps The IIA takes after a pass, or the rules for keeping the certification. Read them on The IIA's Challenge pages when you get there.
